patient.title: Cisplatin + etoposide with radiotherapy
patient.purpose: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy work together to treat limited-stage small-cell lung cancer. Your team explains the aim and why this combined treatment is suitable for you.

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with cell copying. Fluids and kidney checks help reduce harm to healthy tissue.
agents.watch: Report poor fluid intake, reduced urine, ringing in the ears or numbness.

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.mechanism: Disrupts DNA repair during cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide blocks an enzyme cells need while copying DNA. The route and prescribed amount differ between infusion and capsules; they are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.
visual: Disrupts DNA repair during cell division
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, severe mouth soreness or vomiting.

phases.label: Four chemotherapy cycles
phases.detail: Reference plan: four 21-day cycles. Day 1: cisplatin and etoposide. Days 2–3: etoposide. Radiotherapy usually starts with cycle 1; its appointments are planned separately. Capsules, split cisplatin, a 28-day interval or a different platinum are used only if explicitly prescribed.

phases.label: Radiotherapy alongside chemotherapy
phases.detail: Usually begins with cycle 1; later start may be appropriate. The radiation team confirms dose, number of visits and timing. A chemotherapy delay does not automatically mean radiation stops.

phases.label: Recovery and response review
phases.detail: After treatment, your team checks recovery, persistent symptoms and response. Scan type/timing and any useful tumour-marker testing are individual decisions; this regimen does not specify a universal scan or marker timetable.

timeline.label: Cisplatin + etoposide
timeline.text: Reference Day 1 IV treatment plus hydration.

timeline.label: Etoposide Days 2–3
timeline.text: IV each day, or prescribed oral alternative. Split cisplatin only if explicitly prescribed.

timeline.label: Symptoms and separate RT plan
timeline.text: Symptoms may occur on any day. This is not a radiation-fraction schedule or a precise low-blood-count curve.

day_groups.title: Day 1: reference combination
day_groups.body: Blood results, symptoms, anti-sickness medicines and hydration are checked before both drugs.
day_groups.action: Tell the nurse about any hearing, nerve or fluid-intake problems.

day_groups.title: Days 2–3: etoposide
day_groups.body: IV treatment each day or prescribed capsules twice daily. The split-cisplatin alternative changes these visits.
day_groups.action: Use your written prescription; do not add IV and oral etoposide together.

day_groups.title: Support and recovery
day_groups.body: No routine chemotherapy in the reference plan. Follow ongoing anti-sickness medicines and separate RT appointments.
day_groups.action: Call early for poor intake, vomiting, swallowing pain or fever.

day_groups.title: Between chemotherapy cycles
day_groups.body: Fatigue, mouth symptoms and infection risk can persist. RT may continue according to its own plan.
day_groups.action: Report symptoms when they occur; do not wait for the next blood test.

support.title: Fluids and sickness prevention
support.text: Cisplatin needs a planned fluid and anti-sickness course. Follow the labelled medicines for each treatment day and the days afterwards. Call if vomiting prevents drinking or taking medicines.

support.title: If capsules are prescribed
support.text: Etoposide capsules on Days 2–3 replace the IV doses on those days. Take the prescribed amount twice daily on an empty stomach. Follow pharmacy handling instructions and contact the team if a dose is missed or vomited; do not take an extra dose without advice.

support.title: Radiotherapy support
support.text: Ask about swallowing, eating, skin care and fatigue during radiation. Painful swallowing or poor intake needs early help; inability to drink needs urgent assessment.

rationale.summary: Cisplatin crosslinks DNA; etoposide inhibits topoisomeraseII. Radiation causes local DNA damage. Their combined effects are clinically useful but require coordinated marrow, renal, neurologic and oesophageal safety review.
rationale.setting: Limited-stage small-cell lung cancer · combined chemotherapy and radiation
rationale.line: Combined-modality plan selected by multidisciplinary/consultant assessment
factors: Radiation suitability and patient fitness are essential.
alternatives: Other evidence-based local/systemic options, sequential treatment where appropriate, clinical trials and symptom-focused care, according to stage, biomarkers, fitness and preferences.
limitations: The source baseline cisplatin exclusion at CrCl<60 coexists with reduced-dose renal rows; consultant reconciliation is required.
Printed count/renal tables leave small decimal gaps; dose denominators for several toxicity reductions are unspecified.
NCCP00279b is retained clinically, but this patient material and lung trial evidence apply to00279a only.
The cited Turrisi trial used cisplatin60/etoposide120, not NCCP75/100; it studied RT fractionation, not the comparative efficacy of the exact current drug doses.

patient.title: Weekly carboplatin + paclitaxel with radiotherapy
patient.purpose: Chemotherapy is given alongside radiotherapy to treat stage III non-small-cell lung cancer when cisplatin is unsuitable. Your team explains the treatment aim and choices.

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Paclitaxel stabilises structures needed for cell division. It can also affect nerves, blood cells and healthy tissues. Premedicines help reduce infusion reactions.
agents.watch: Report numbness, tingling, muscle/joint pain or new breathing symptoms.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with cell copying. Its dose uses kidney filtration and target exposure(AUC), not a fixed number of milligrams.
agents.watch: Report fever, unusual bleeding, vomiting or allergy symptoms.

phases.label: Seven weekly chemotherapy treatments
phases.detail: Both medicines are given by drip once every 7 days for seven weeks, alongside a separate radiotherapy course. The plan may change for side effects or test results. Further chemotherapy after radiotherapy is a separate decision.

phases.label: Radiation course
phases.detail: Radiation is given during the chemotherapy course. Its dose, number of fractions and precise timing are prescribed by radiation oncology. A chemotherapy delay does not automatically stop radiation.

phases.label: After chemoradiation
phases.detail: Your team reviews recovery and response. NCCP describes optional separate two-cycle carboplatin/paclitaxel consolidation under00304; it is not automatically included and any next treatment needs a separate prescription.

timeline.label: Paclitaxel then carboplatin
timeline.text: One weekly chemotherapy visit after blood tests and premedicines.

timeline.label: Symptoms and separate RT plan
timeline.text: Continue the written radiation and support plan. Symptoms may occur on any day; this is not a radiation-fraction calendar.

day_groups.title: Weekly treatment day
day_groups.body: Blood results and symptoms are reviewed. Paclitaxel comes first, followed by carboplatin.
day_groups.action: Tell staff immediately about flushing, breathing trouble, pain or swelling during infusion.

day_groups.title: Support at home
day_groups.body: Use the anti-sickness medicines prescribed for these days. Radiation visits may continue on their own schedule.
day_groups.action: Call for fever, poor intake, vomiting or new breathing symptoms.

day_groups.title: Before the next weekly dose
day_groups.body: Keep track of swallowing, fatigue, numbness and muscle/joint symptoms. Arrange the next weekly blood tests.
day_groups.action: Report problems before the next dose; do not wait if acutely unwell.

support.title: Weekly medicines before treatment
support.text: Paclitaxel needs premedicines to reduce allergic reactions. The first week and later weeks can differ. Your team also provides anti-sickness medicines for carboplatin; do not double up steroid doses.

support.title: Eating, swallowing and breathing
support.text: Chest radiation can make swallowing sore. Ask early for pain relief and nutrition support. New breathlessness, cough or inability to drink needs urgent advice, even after the course finishes.

support.title: Nerves and aches
support.text: Tell the team about numbness, tingling or muscle/joint pain before each weekly visit. Follow the agreed pain-relief plan and check before starting medicines or supplements.

rationale.setting: Stage III non-small-cell lung cancer · concurrent chemoradiation
rationale.line: Combined-modality plan selected by multidisciplinary/consultant assessment
factors: Radiation suitability and patient fitness are essential.
alternatives: Other evidence-based local/systemic options, sequential treatment where appropriate, clinical trials and symptom-focused care, according to stage, biomarkers, fitness and preferences.
limitations: Baseline counts differ from on-treatment counts; platelets exactly75 and the baseline ANC1.5 boundary require reconciliation.
Paclitaxel product-information retreatment counts are higher than the NCCP weekly table; the tool flags disagreement.
Paclitaxel ALT/bilirubin bands contain decimal gaps; severe liver impairment remains a separate exclusion.
NCCP calls the treatment section adjuvant but the indication is StageIII NSCLC and cited evidence includes inoperable disease; do not infer required surgery or a universal postoperative setting.
The Choy study is small, single-arm and included two subsequent consolidation cycles; outcomes cannot isolate weekly chemoradiation or be used as an individual prognosis.

key_points: Both medicines are given by drip once every 7 days for seven weeks, alongside a separate radiotherapy course. The plan may change for side effects or test results. Further chemotherapy after radiotherapy is a separate decision.
Blood count, kidney and liver tests before treatment. Measured kidney filtration is preferred, or a verified estimate. Hearing and nerve assessment if clinically indicated.
Blood count with differential, kidney and liver tests every week. Check nerve symptoms if indicated. If GFR is calculated, creatinine must be within 48 hours of carboplatin.

After treatment, your team checks recovery, persistent symptoms and response. Scan type/timing and any useful tumour-marker testing are individual decisions; this regimen does not specify a universal scan or marker timetable.

patient_selection.treatment_intent: Chemotherapy is given alongside radiotherapy to treat stage III non-small-cell lung cancer when cisplatin is unsuitable. Your team explains the treatment aim and choices.
disease_and_biomarker_context: No biomarker-specific eligibility is specified for this cytotoxic chemoradiation protocol; do not invent one.
eligibility_orientation: StageIII NSCLC; ECOG0–2; unsuitable for cisplatin because of comorbidity/renal function; adequate organ function, baseline ANC>1.5 and platelets≥100.
Hypersensitivity; pregnancy/breastfeeding; severe hepatic impairment; baseline neutrophils<1.5; significant pleural effusions.

support_summary: Paclitaxel needs premedicines to reduce allergic reactions. The first week and later weeks can differ. Your team also provides anti-sickness medicines for carboplatin; do not double up steroid doses.
Chest radiation can make swallowing sore. Ask early for pain relief and nutrition support. New breathlessness, cough or inability to drink needs urgent advice, even after the course finishes.
Tell the team about numbness, tingling or muscle/joint pain before each weekly visit. Follow the agreed pain-relief plan and check before starting medicines or supplements.

ongoing: After treatment, your team checks recovery, persistent symptoms and response. Scan type/timing and any useful tumour-marker testing are individual decisions; this regimen does not specify a universal scan or marker timetable.
Review RT coordination, infection, hydration, swallowing, respiratory symptoms and cumulative toxicity.
administration: Paclitaxel is infused first over one hour, then carboplatin over 30 minutes, plus checks and premedicines. The consultant may prescribe a lower paclitaxel dose. RT appointments are separate and are not counted as chemotherapy doses.
access: Appropriate IV access, anaphylaxis equipment and trained staff; monitor infusion site and vital symptoms.
Radiation oncology prescribes RT dose/fractions and confirms any interruptions.

evidence.population: 40 previously untreated inoperable locally advanced NSCLC patients enrolled;39 eligible,37 assessable for response/toxicity.
evidence.comparison: Single-arm paclitaxel50 mg/m² plus carboplatinAUC2 weekly for 7 weeks with66 Gy/33 fractions, followed by two q3week paclitaxel200 mg/m²/carboplatinAUC6 cycles.
evidence.applicability: Matches the weekly drug doses but studied a combined course including consolidation. Trial RT details describe the study; they are not imposed on the current patient plan.

endpoints.interpretation: Single-arm activity signal, not evidence of comparative benefit.

evidence.qualitative_result: Activity was observed, with substantial oesophagitis; randomised confirmation was required.

support_plans.label: Week 1 · antiemetic plus paclitaxel reaction prevention

medicines.name: Dexamethasone antiemetic reference
medicines.note: Reconcile with paclitaxel steroid premedication; one approved schedule.

medicines.name: Metoclopramide
medicines.dose: 10 mg orally three times daily as needed

medicines.name: Dexamethasone paclitaxel reference
medicines.note: NCCP reaction-prevention dose; do not duplicate the antiemetic steroid.

additional_support: Reconcile paclitaxel premedication and antiemetic dexamethasone into ONE prescription; do not add duplicate steroids.
NCCP allows consultant-led famotidine omission without prior hypersensitivity, while noting uncertain reaction risk; close monitoring and reaction facilities remain necessary.
Muscle/joint pain: consider prescribed analgesia. Assess swallowing, nutrition and respiratory symptoms during and after RT.
No routine G-CSF, antibiotic, antiviral or PJP prophylaxis is mandated in this source; assess individual risk/local policy.
